title: Improving productivity in Hollywood with data science: Using emotional arcs of movies to drive product and service innovation in entertainment industries
venue: Journal of the Operational Research Society
finding: Per authors, emotional trajectories extracted from 6,174 movie scripts cluster into 6 basic shapes; the highest box office is associated with the 'Man in a Hole' arc (emotional fall followed by a rise), irrespective of genre and production budget.
why_for_us: Shape each 60-90 s episode (and the 8-episode season) as fall-then-rise: open on a problem at the notary's desk, end on relief or a win.

title: Narrative reversals and story success
finding: Per authors, across 30,000 movies, TV shows, novels and fundraising pitches, narrative reversals measured as shifts in valence predict success: stories with more, and more dramatic, turning points are more successful.
why_for_us: Plan at least one clear reversal per episode (good-to-bad or bad-to-good) and make it large; count reversals per script as a writing check.

title: What Makes Content Engaging? How Emotional Dynamics Shape Success
finding: Per authors, automated sentiment analysis of over 4,000 movies shows that more sentiment-volatile movies are evaluated more positively (stronger in thrillers than romance); over 30,000 online articles show people keep reading more volatile texts; follow-up experiments manipulating volatility support a causal effect via stimulation.
why_for_us: Alternate positive and negative beats shot to shot instead of holding one mood; a flat-tone episode is the risk, not a 'too busy' one.

title: The speed of stories: Semantic progression and narrative success.
finding: Per authors, in over 40,000 movie scripts, movies with slower semantic progression early and faster semantic progression later are evaluated more positively; analysis of over 10,000 TV episodes finds similar results.
why_for_us: Stay in one situation at the start of an episode so viewers orient, then accelerate topic and scene changes toward the end.

title: How quantifying the shape of stories predicts their success
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
finding: Per authors, texts (movies, TV shows, academic papers) can be represented as paths in a latent semantic space and simple measures of that path are linked to success, with important differences between domains; the abstract does not state the direction of effects for movies and TV.
why_for_us: Gives a measurable vocabulary (how fast, how much ground, how circuitous) for comparing our scripts; rules must be read from the full paper, not assumed across formats.

title: Narrative theory and the dynamics of popular movies
finding: Per author, corpus analysis in 12 studies shows popular movies divide into 4 acts (setup, complication, development, climax) with optional prolog and epilog and a few turning points; patterns of shot duration, transitions, scale, motion, luminance, character introduction, conversation, music and action reduce to 5 correlated stylistic dimensions.
why_for_us: Use a compressed four-part skeleton per episode (setup, complication, development, climax) and let shot length, music and shot scale change with the part.

title: From Story Line to Box Office: A New Approach for Green-Lighting Movie Scripts
finding: Per authors, a model combining screenwriting domain knowledge, natural-language processing and statistical learning forecasts a movie's return on investment from script text alone and, in a holdout decision task, significantly improves a studio's gross ROI.
why_for_us: Script-level features carry measurable signal before production, which supports scoring our episode scripts against a checklist before spending on AI video generation.

title: Investigating Responses to Narrative Cliffhangers Using Affective Disposition Theory
finding: Per authors, in two between-subjects experiments (N=202; N=273) with written narratives, cliffhanger endings increased desire for a future installment versus a protagonist victory (both studies) and an antagonist victory (Study 2), with no significant differences in enjoyment or suspense.
why_for_us: End episodes 1-7 on an unresolved question: it raises the wish for the next episode without a measurable enjoyment cost; resolve fully only in episode 8.

title: FACTORS INVOLVED IN GENERATING SUSPENSE
finding: Per authors, in a factorial experiment with an audiovisual chase sequence, rated suspense was highest when the hero's chances of success were perceived as about 1 in 100 and minimal when success or failure seemed certain; suspense also increased with more positive disposition toward the protagonist.
why_for_us: Make the protagonist's success look nearly but not fully impossible (deadline in minutes, missing document), and establish that she is likeable before the threat.

title: Mystery Appeal: Effects of Uncertainty and Resolution on the Enjoyment of Mystery
finding: Per authors (N=84, manipulated short story), enjoyment was greater when readers were highly uncertain about the culprit and felt high curiosity; enjoyment of the resolution depended on resolution type and self-esteem (confirmation disliked by high self-esteem readers, surprise disliked by low self-esteem readers).
why_for_us: Keep two plausible explanations open through the season (who altered the deed?) and avoid a finale that only confirms the obvious for an expert audience.

title: Story Spoilers Don’t Spoil Stories
finding: The OpenAlex abstract describes three experiments with stories from different genres testing spoilers and argues that foreknowledge may raise processing fluency; a later retrieved replication (Daniel & Katz 2018) summarises the result as spoiled stories being enjoyed as much as or more than unspoiled ones.
why_for_us: Showing the outcome first (a cold open with the signed deed, then 'how we got here') is not automatically harmful; treat it as a testable variant.

title: Spoiler Alert: Consequences of Narrative Spoilers for Dimensions of Enjoyment, Appreciation, and Transportation
finding: Per authors, in a within-subjects experiment (N=412) unspoiled stories were more fun and suspenseful and also more moving and enjoyable in general; no effect on media choice emerged.
why_for_us: Default to not revealing the episode outcome in titles, thumbnails or captions.

title: (Don’t) Tell Me How It Ends: Spoilers, Enjoyment, and Involvement in Television and Film
finding: Per authors, across two experiments and a survey with audiovisual material, spoilers for television and film had quite small and qualified effects; genre and involvement moderated negative effects, and spoilers for upcoming films triggered reactance more than they changed enjoyment or viewing intentions.
why_for_us: Spoiler effects are small either way, so choose teaser and recap content for clarity and curiosity rather than out of fear of giving things away.

title: Spoilers Affect the Enjoyment of Television Episodes but Not Short Stories
finding: Per authors, Experiment 1 (short stories) and Experiment 2 (full-length television episodes) differed from earlier positive spoiler findings: under certain circumstances spoilers had a negative effect on enjoyment for television but not for short stories.
why_for_us: For video, lean toward protecting the twist; findings from text stories do not transfer cleanly to screen episodes.

title: Binge-Watching: A Suspenseful, Emotional, Habit
finding: Per authors (survey, N=797, students plus a representative adult sample), binge-watching frequency is driven largely by existing habit, with suspense and anticipation tied to the content and emotion-regulation motives as further significant antecedents; appointment viewing was driven by viewing efficacy and older age.
why_for_us: Build a habit cue (fixed publishing day, same opening sting) and carry anticipation across episodes; both independently predict continued viewing.

title: The More You Watch, the More You Get? Re-Examining the Effects of Binge-Watching on Entertainment Experiences
venue: Journal of Media Psychology Theories Methods and Applications
finding: Per authors, in an experiment (n=80) binge-watching had slightly negative effects on transportation, hedonic entertainment and valence but a positive effect on arousal; in a field study with tracking data (n=47) there were no differences, so binge-watching per se does not affect the entertainment experience.
why_for_us: Episodes must work both watched alone and back to back; do not count on a season-drop to lift enjoyment.

title: The impact of binge watching on memory and perceived comprehension
finding: Per authors, in a controlled study binge-watching produced strong memory right after viewing but faster decay than daily or weekly viewing schedules, and binge viewers reported significantly less show enjoyment than daily or weekly viewers.
why_for_us: If the goal is that notaries remember the product, a spaced release (daily or weekly) is the safer schedule than dropping all 8 episodes at once.

title: The Effect of Binge-Watching on the Subscription of Video on Demand: Results from Randomized Experiments
finding: Per authors, in two randomized field experiments households induced to binge-watch were less likely to pay for subscription video on demand after free trials, apparently because they depleted content of interest quickly; recommendation reminders that widened preferences offset the effect.
why_for_us: A fast-consumed 8-episode season leaves nothing to return for; pace the release and point finished viewers to the next thing (demo, season 2 teaser).

title: Antecedents and Effects of Parasocial Relationships: A Meta-Analysis
finding: Per authors, a meta-analysis of four decades of research (k=120) finds no significant relationship between social deficiencies and parasocial relationships (PSRs); PSRs correlate strongly with homophily, identification, transportation and persuasive outcomes, and only moderately with parasocial interaction.
why_for_us: Make the lead recognisably 'one of us' for notaries and their staff (same tasks, same pressures); perceived similarity is what feeds the bond and the persuasion.

title: Defining Identification: A Theoretical Look at the Identification of Audiences With Media Characters
finding: Theoretical article: defines identification with media characters, distinguishes it from other audience reactions to characters, and derives hypotheses about its antecedents and consequences.
why_for_us: Decide per character whether we want viewers to be her (identification: stay in her point of view) or to be with her (parasocial: address the camera); the two call for different staging.

title: Expanding Disposition Theory: Reconsidering Character Liking, Moral Evaluations, and Enjoyment
finding: Theoretical article: uses schema theory to propose alternative ways viewers form strong feelings toward characters and examines how viewers perpetuate and defend those feelings for the sake of enjoyment.
why_for_us: With 60-90 s we cannot earn liking slowly; lean on instantly readable character schemas (overworked junior, exacting notary) so dispositions form in the first seconds.

title: When Good Characters Do Bad Things: Examining the Effect of Moral Ambiguity on Enjoyment
finding: Per authors (experiment, N=313), good characters are enjoyed because they are liked; bad characters are liked least but are equally transporting and suspenseful; morally ambiguous characters are liked less than good ones yet are equally transporting, suspenseful, cognitively engaging and enjoyable.
why_for_us: A flawed but competent protagonist (cuts a corner, then fixes it) costs some liking but not engagement, and fits a profession with strict duties.

title: Morality Predicts Enjoyment But Not Appreciation of Morally Ambiguous Characters
finding: Per authors (survey, N=294), self-expansion, wishful identification and moral violation were all strongly related to enjoyment of characters, whereas appreciation was not related to moral violation.
why_for_us: Give the lead a quality viewers would like to have (calm under pressure, mastery of the tools); wishful identification drives enjoyment.

title: Exploring How We Enjoy Antihero Narratives
finding: Per authors, three studies indicate moral judgment matters less for antihero enjoyment than affective disposition theory predicts, prior exposure to an antihero narrative alters responses to similar ones, and moral disengagement cues affect enjoyment.
why_for_us: If a character bends rules, supply a justification cue in the same scene; in a compliance-minded audience, unexcused rule-breaking will read as the product endorsing it.

title: When Good Friends Say Goodbye: A Parasocial Breakup Study
finding: Per authors (survey of 279 students after the last episode of Friends), intensity of the parasocial relationship with the favourite character was the strongest predictor of breakup distress; commitment and affinity to the show, the character's perceived popularity and loneliness also predicted it.
why_for_us: Keep the same faces across all 8 episodes and across seasons; attachment is to a character, and replacing her resets it.

title: Identification with characters and narrative persuasion through fictional feature films
finding: Per author, three studies: identification with characters was associated with enjoyment of feature films across genres, predicted the affective impact and cognitive elaboration of a dramatic film, and predicted a full-length fiction film's incidental impact on attitudes and beliefs.
why_for_us: The product message should arrive through what the identified-with character does and feels, not through a voice-over claim.

title: Beloved Bingeable Breakups? The Impact of Binge Watching on Retrospective Imaginative Involvement, Parasocial Relationships, and Parasocial Breakups
finding: Per authors (quantitative mixed-design study), binge-watching positively predicted retrospective imaginative involvement, which predicted positive but not negative parasocial relationships; both positive and negative PSRs predicted parasocial breakup intensity.
why_for_us: Give viewers something to think about between episodes (an open question about a character); post-viewing imagining is the route from viewing to attachment.

title: Appreciation as Audience Response: Exploring Entertainment Gratifications Beyond Hedonism
finding: Per authors, three studies of film viewing identify and measure gratifications of fun and suspense and also of moving, thought-provoking experience (appreciation), with all three leading to perceptions of a more lasting or enduring effect.
why_for_us: Aim each episode at one of three payoffs on purpose (laugh, tension, or a moving moment about why the work matters) and track which one viewers report.

title: Entertainment as Pleasurable and Meaningful: Identifying Hedonic and Eudaimonic Motivations for Entertainment Consumption
finding: Per authors, four studies develop and validate measures showing that people choose entertainment for pleasure-seeking (hedonic) and for truth-seeking (eudaimonic) reasons, and that these motivations predict preferences for entertainment eliciting distinct affective experiences.
why_for_us: A professional audience will include meaning-seekers; at least one episode should show the human stake behind a notarial act, not only office comedy.

title: The Role of Cognitive and Affective Challenge in Entertainment Experience
finding: Per authors (2x2 experiment), cognitive and affective challenge produced stronger appreciation of a movie, affective challenge heightened suspense, and the absence of both fostered the experience of fun.
why_for_us: Pick the lever per episode: keep it easy for a fun episode, add an emotional or intellectual difficulty for one meant to be remembered.

title: Mood Management in the Context of Selective Exposure Theory
venue: Annals of the International Communication Association
finding: Theoretical chapter: proposes that hedonistic motivation, as articulated in mood-management theory, dominates spontaneous entertainment choices, while choice of informational content is dominated by informational utility with non-informational anticipations as a complement.
why_for_us: Notaries will meet the series in a break, as entertainment: lead with mood repair (relief, recognition, a laugh) and let product information ride along.

title: Who’s Laughing Now? The Effect of Simulated Laughter on Consumer Enjoyment of Television Comedies and the Laugh-Track Paradox
venue: Journal of the Association for Consumer Research
finding: Per authors, three experimentally controlled field studies show simulated laughter increases perception of a programme as humorous but at the same time limits viewers' ability to transport into the narrative (a competitive mediation termed the 'laugh-track paradox').
why_for_us: Do not add canned laughter or reaction stingers; they cue 'funny' but pull viewers out of the story we need them inside.

title: Social facilitation and laughter in media: meta-analysis of the impact of laugh tracks
finding: Per authors, a meta-analysis of experiments across 35 manuscripts finds an average positive effect of adding a laugh track on positive reaction (r=.391), including number of laughs (r=.241), laughter duration (r=.442) and self-reported enjoyment (r=.311).
why_for_us: Audible laughter does raise laughing; if we want that lift, put it inside the scene (a colleague cracking up) rather than as an external track.

title: The Language of Laughter: A Quantitative/Qualitative Fusion Examining Television Narrative and Humor
finding: Per authors, in an experiment on four episodes of 'The Andy Griffith Show', the episode highest in perceived humour and enjoyment was the only one where the laugh track had a negative impact; it had a more complex story structure and higher levels of satire.
why_for_us: Invest in story structure and satire of real office absurdities; well-built comedy does not need laughter cues and is hurt by them.

title: Enjoyment of Unoriginal Characters: Individual Differences in Nostalgia-Proneness and Parasocial Relationships
finding: Per authors (experiment with storyboards), stronger parasocial relationships with characters predicted greater parasocial interaction, enjoyment and viewing intentions; results partially showed that nostalgia-prone participants expressed greater enjoyment and viewing intentions for familiar characters.
why_for_us: Familiar office artefacts (the old repertory book, a dot-matrix printer, the 'Komputerku' address itself) can add enjoyment for nostalgia-prone viewers; use as seasoning.

title: Attention and the Evolution of Hollywood Film
finding: Per authors, shot-length sequences of 150 Hollywood films released 1935-2005 show that over 70 years shots became increasingly correlated in length with their neighbours, producing power spectra approaching 1/f, which the authors suggest may help harness attention to the narrative.
why_for_us: Vary shot length in waves (runs of short shots, then a run of longer ones) rather than cutting on a metronome.

title: Shot Durations, Shot Classes, and the Increased Pace of Popular Movies
finding: Per authors, mean shot duration in 9,400 English-language and 1,550 non-English-language movies (1912-2013) shows a linear decline on a logarithmic scale in the sound era; 25 percent of the decline is due to a shift toward shot classes with shorter durations and 8 percent to shot scales in which characters appear larger.
why_for_us: Short shots and closer framing on faces are the long-run direction of popular film and suit a vertical phone frame; default to medium close-ups.

title: Neurocinematics: The Neuroscience of Film
finding: Per authors, fMRI inter-subject correlation during free viewing shows some films exert considerable control over viewers' brain activity and eye movements, and the level of control differs with movie content, editing and directing style.
why_for_us: Tightly directed, clearly staged footage makes viewers respond alike; loose, unstructured AI shots give up that control.

title: Audience preferences are predicted by temporal reliability of neural processing
finding: Per authors, the level of inter-subject correlation in EEG responses of a small group watching previously broadcast television content predicts expressions of interest and preference among thousands (social media activity and audience ratings), and predicts the larger audience more accurately than the tested individuals themselves.
why_for_us: Moments that make all viewers react the same way predict population preference; one unambiguous focus per shot is the practical proxy.

title: The Impact of Continuity Editing in Narrative Film on Event Segmentation: Cognitive Science
finding: Per authors (segmentation task with fMRI on a commercial film), discontinuities in action had the biggest impact on perceived event boundaries, while discontinuities in space and time had minor effects.
why_for_us: We can jump location and time freely inside 60-90 s as long as the action stays continuous; change the action only where a new beat should be felt.

title: What Would Jaws Do? The Tyranny of Film and the Relationship between Gaze and Higher-Level Narrative Film Comprehension
finding: Per authors, viewers who saw the preceding 2.5 minutes before a 12-second clip were more likely to draw the critical predictive inference and to perceive coherence across the 6-shot sequence than viewers who saw only the clip, while attentional synchrony of gaze was strong in both conditions.
why_for_us: Where people look is set by the image, but understanding needs context: a 3-5 s recap or a line of setup at the top of each episode pays for itself.

title: Viewers' Interpretations of Film Characters' Emotions: Effects of Presenting Film Music Before or After a Character is Shown
finding: Per authors (177 undergraduates), viewers interpreted emotionally neutral film characters' emotions consistently with the emotion of music played before or after the scene, evidence of forward and backward affective priming.
why_for_us: Music can set the emotional reading of an AI-generated face with a neutral expression; place the cue just before or just after the shot.

title: Arousing the audience: The two-peak structure of drama film trailers
finding: Per authors, an exploratory skin-conductance study of four drama film trailers indicates that recall, evaluation and desire to see the film depend less on overall arousal than on a pattern with variation and build-up to memorable scenes; a two-peak structure is suggested as the optimal arousal curve.
why_for_us: A trailer-length episode can carry two arousal peaks (an early hook and a late climax) with a dip between; do not try to hold maximum intensity throughout.

title: Television Viewing and Public Perceptions of Attorneys
finding: Per authors, prime-time network depictions of attorneys affect public perceptions of attorneys, particularly for front-region behaviours, and content-specific viewing is a more reliable predictor of these perceptions than total viewing or sociodemographic variables.
why_for_us: Fiction about a legal profession shapes how that profession is seen; notaries will judge the series partly as a statement about them, so the on-screen conduct has to be defensible.

title: Television Exposure and the Public's Perceptions of Physicians
finding: Per authors, exposure to prime-time doctor shows was negatively related to perceptions of physicians, consistent with the prediction that newer, less flattering medical shows lower regard for doctors.
why_for_us: Comedy that makes the notary look incompetent or venal can cost the profession regard; aim the jokes at the situation and the paperwork.

title: The Effects of Viewing Grey's Anatomy on Perceptions of Doctors and Patient Satisfaction
finding: Per author, heavy viewers of Grey's Anatomy perceived the programme as credible; credibility was positively associated with perceiving real doctors as courageous (an indirect effect of viewing mediated through credibility), which was positively associated with patient satisfaction.
why_for_us: Perceived credibility is the gate for any effect on attitudes; one procedural error a notary would spot can close it.

title: A Study of Juror Expectations and Demands Concerning Scientific Evidence: Does the “CSI Effect” Exist?
venue: Vanderbilt Journal of Entertainment & Technology Law
finding: Per authors, a survey of 1,027 persons called for jury duty found significant expectations and demands for scientific evidence but little or no link between them and watching particular television shows; the authors suggest a broader 'tech effect' in popular culture.
why_for_us: Do not expect a short series alone to shift what professionals expect of technology; it can ride an existing expectation that offices should be digital.

title: You Can't Take Fingerprints Off Water: Police Officers' Views Toward "Cop" Television Shows
finding: Per author (816 police officers, data described as tentative), officers preferred police shows that stressed professionalism, discussed as reality of the episode, believability of characters and dialogue, and correctness of procedure; interesting dialogue, humour and correct procedure were cited repeatedly for the top-rated show.
why_for_us: Professionals reward depictions that show them as competent and get procedure right, and they welcome humour alongside it; have a practising notary review every script.

title: Les policiers réels devant leurs homologues fictifs : fiction impossible ?
finding: Per author (three-month ethnographic study in urban police), officers are ambivalent toward police series: they largely accuse them of tarnishing the profession's reputation and creating confusion about its status, powers and mission, yet series that resonate with their work experience can anchor professional identity.
why_for_us: Build scenes from real, recognisable office moments so notaries and staff say 'that is us'; avoid anything that blurs what a notary may and may not do.

title: Narrative Complexity in Contemporary American Television
finding: Essay (the OpenAlex abstract is in Portuguese): describes a storytelling model in American television since the 1990s that uses narrative complexity as an alternative to conventional episodic and serial forms, and examines its formal features, modes of viewing and comprehension, and reasons for its emergence.
why_for_us: Combine a self-contained case per episode with one season-long thread, so each episode is complete for a new viewer and still rewards those who follow the series.
